newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico hikes minimum wage, but prices also soar.
newsitem.headline: Mexico hikes minimum wage, but prices also soar.

text.p: Mexico Tuesday took a stab at mending years of falling real wages by raising the minimum wage 17 percent, but for most Mexicans the move was marred by sharp increases in transportation and energy costs.

In the run-up to Christmas, economists said the wage hike was significant in that it formed the basis for higher yearly bonuses, and was also above the government's 15 percent inflation target for 1997.

There was a catch, however, and few workers were blind to it. Hardly any Mexican economists expected the government to meet its 15 percent inflation target next year, and the consensus forecast is for an inflation rate above 17 percent.

Five leaders of an anti-government independent union have staged a seven-day hunger strike against the wage hike, chaining themselves to the gates of the National Minimum Wage Commission offices. On Monday, they drew their own blood to signify the drain on real wages.

For almost two decades, Mexican union leaders say minimum wage increases have lagged inflation, eroding purchasing power in a trend that was exacerbated by Mexico's 1995 economic crisis and the worst recession in 50 years.
Tuesday's increase raised it to a maximum 26.45 pesos a day, or about $3.36. It was part of a wage and prices pact signed between government, business and labour in October.

"The rise is in some ways a good sign," said Guillermo Valdes, a labour economist at Mexico City-based think tank Grupo Economistas y Asociados. "For the first time (in years), there is a minimum salary fixed above projected inflation."

"But average inflation next year will be above 15 percent. You're still going to have a slight real loss in purchasing power," he added. Only some 3.5 million workers earn the minimum wage, but most wages in the 35-million strong workforce are loosely tied to it.

For workers, the wage hike was offset by a slew of price rises that took effect last weekend and caused widespread grumbling in the capital. Fuel prices went up 8 percent from Dec.1, and are slated to rise 22 percent in 1997.

Urban transport rose from 20 percent to 50 percent, including a 30 percent increase in the price of the subsidised "metro" underground train system, used daily by 4.2 million of the capital's 17 million inhabitants.

With an eye on critical mid-term elections next year, pro-government Mexican union bosses had bargained for a higher minimum wage increase than 17 percent, but they typically shrugged off their defeat as inevitable.
"We had to accept it," 96-year-old labour leader Fidel Velazquez of the powerful Mexican Workers Confederation told a news conference on Monday.

Prior to the wage hike, Velazquez had threatened to withdraw his union from the National Minimum Wage Commission if the 17 percent hike was not increased. But as usual in a country where his union has always been a backbone of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), his threats came to nothing.
